key_findings.value: HR shows a laminated microstructure of δ-ferrite (δ-F) bands alternating with lath martensite (M); α-ferrite (α-F) and M are visible at higher magnification and small retained austenite (RA) regions lie inside the martensite bands (Fig. 3a, b; 50 µm and 10 µm scale bars).

measurement_conditions.value: Metallographic specimens mechanically polished (PG-1A polishing machine) and etched in 10 % nitric acid alcohol; room temperature.

purpose.value: Observe and analyse the microstructure of the hot-rolled (HR) state.

source.reason: SEM of HR is described in section 3.2 and Fig. 3(a,b); instrument and preparation are in b0020.

instrument_or_setup.value: EBSD (Oxford Instruments) probe with FE-SEM; HKL Channel5 software and Python for data analysis.

key_findings.value: By EBSD the HR austenite volume fraction is ~16 %; austenite (red) is concentrated in patchy bands inside the martensitic regions; HR has the highest KAM signal of the six conditions and GND densities of 10.81 × 10^14 m^-2 (BCC) and 8.37 × 10^14 m^-2 (FCC).

measurement_conditions.value: Specimens electrochemically polished in electrolyte of 10 % perchloric acid, 5 % glycerol and 85 % ethyl alcohol (15~20 V, 0.8–1.2 A); EBSD step size 150 nm.

boundary_and_initial_conditions.value: Equilibrium calculation for the Fe–9Mn–5Al-0.3C (wt.%) steel over ~500–1600 °C (phase fractions) and ~500–1400 °C (Mn/Al/C mass fractions in ferrite and austenite).

simulation_method.value: equilibrium thermodynamic (CALPHAD) phase-fraction and composition-partitioning calculation

source.reason: Thermo-Calc with TCFE 12 was used to compute the equilibrium phase volume-fraction diagram (Fig. 2) and the C/Al/Mn partitioning used to justify heat-treatment temperatures; this calculation applies to the steel that includes the HR state.

validation_against_experiment.value: Used to select the quenching and intercritical annealing temperatures; the calculated A1 (cementite precipitation) temperature of ~617 °C and the maximum austenite fraction (~91.4 % at ~970 °C) guided the experimental temperatures, with an acknowledged discrepancy of the software.

interface_notes.value: The report notes that hardness difference between δ-ferrite band and tempered-martensite lamellar leads to stress concentration at their interfaces; crack-related interface behaviour is described mainly for the annealed (QA) fracture surfaces, not measured separately on HR.

phase_evolution.value: During hot rolling in the dual-phase region a dual-phase layered microstructure of δ-ferrite and austenite formed; on cooling to room temperature the weakly stable austenite underwent martensitic transformation, giving α-ferrite and lath martensite, with retained austenite remaining in the martensite bands (Mf of the steel below room temperature).

source.reason: The HR state has a δ-ferrite/martensite laminated structure (b0028); the general δ-ferrite-band / martensite-interface stress-concentration statement is in the deformation discussion (b0078). Coherence across this interface is not reported.

comparison_metric.value: The hot-rolled (HR) reference state provides the strongest but least ductile baseline: highest TS (~1107 MPa) and lowest PSE (6.2 ± 0.6 GPa %) among all studied states, used as the benchmark against which the intercritical quenching-annealing (QA) conditions are compared.

source.reason: The HR state is presented as the hot-rolled reference/baseline whose mechanical properties (highest TS, poorest elongation, lowest PSE) are compared against IQ-1050 and QA specimens (Table 3, section 3.3).

overall_structure.value: Micro-laminated (banded) microstructure consisting of δ-ferrite (δ-F) bands and lath martensite (M) lamellar, produced by thermomechanical rolling in the dual-phase region; retained austenite (RA) observed in the martensite bands, and α-ferrite (α-F) also formed on cooling.

source.reason: The HR state is described in section 3.2 (Fig. 3a,b) as a laminated microstructure of δ-ferrite bands and lath martensite with retained austenite; Table 2 gives the HR austenite fraction (~16% by EBSD) and Fig. 8(a) gives the HR GND densities; Fig. 7(a-1) gives the HR KAM.

unmapped_findings: HR (hot-rolled) exhibited the highest tensile strength, 1107 ± 32 MPa, but poor ductility, 5.6 ± 0.4 %, attributed to its highest GND densities (BCC 10.81 × 10^14 m^-2, FCC 8.37 × 10^14 m^-2) arising from the relatively larger ferrite content (b0051).

In HR the retained austenite distribution is more concentrated (patchy bands within the martensitic regions) than in the QA specimens; the γ/α boundary density of IQ-1050 was higher than that of HR (b0031, b0059).
The Mf temperature of the experimental steel was lower than room temperature, as indicated by retained austenite observed in the martensite bands of the HR state (b0028).

HR showed the highest values of sub-block boundary density and of low-/high-angle packet boundary density among the conditions according to Fig. 8(b), whereas block boundary density of HR was lower than that of IQ-1050 (b0059, figure_008).
The steel density 7.34 g·cm^-3 (Archimedes drainage method), 6.7 % lower than low-carbon low-alloyed steels, applies to the whole experimental steel including the HR state (b0016).
